explanations.explanation: A colt it is, friend. Jesus tells the two disciples they'll find one tied there, in the village ahead of them. They go and find it just as He told them (Luke 19:32). Every detail He gave, they got to check, and every detail held up.
A ram would make a LOUD entrance, I'll give you that. But Jesus says they'll find a colt tied in the village. The two disciples go and find it just as He told them. No horns needed, friend.

A camel would be a tall order, friend, and I mean that literally. Jesus says the two will find a colt tied in the village ahead. The text says they found it just as He told them. Nobody had to look up for this one.
True! Jesus says it's a colt “on which no one has ever sat.” That's a very specific detail to give two people who haven't even left yet. And then, just as He said, they find it.

The text says the opposite, friend. Jesus tells them it's a colt “on which no one has ever sat.” That's right there in Luke 19:30. It's one of those details you could check for yourself, and the two disciples found it just as He told them.

That's it. Jesus says, “If anyone asks, ‘Why are you untying it?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it.’” Short and simple, the kind of answer you could say with a straight face. And when the owners do ask, the disciples answer, “The Lord needs it,” word for word (Luke 19:34).

explanations.answer: We will bring it back soon
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a polite thing to say, friend, but Jesus never tells them to say it. The text gives them four words: “The Lord needs it.” I've gotta say, that's a lot shorter than the speech I'd have prepared. And that's exactly what the disciples say when the owners ask (Luke 19:34).
Nope, no neighbor in this story, friend. Jesus tells them to say, “The Lord needs it.” That's the whole answer. The disciples say exactly that when the owners ask them (Luke 19:34).

Owners, yes! The text says, “As they were untying the colt, its owners asked, ‘Why are you untying the colt?’” So somebody was home, and somebody noticed. Good thing the disciples already had their answer ready.

Servants is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word in the text. Luke 19:33 says it was the colt's owners who asked. I think anybody would ask if strangers were untying their colt. And the disciples had their answer ready.
Neighbors would be a nosy bunch, friend, but the text says owners. Luke 19:33 says, “its owners asked.” It makes sense they'd be the ones asking. The disciples answered just the way Jesus told them.

Their cloaks, friend! Luke 19:35 says they “threw their cloaks over it, and put Jesus on it.” No saddle in sight, so the disciples used what they were wearing. Think of it like packing the cookie box with your own apron because you ran out of paper.
Sackcloth isn't in this story, friend. The disciples threw their cloaks over the colt, then put Jesus on it. That's right there in Luke 19:35. They used what they had on them.

Fine linen sounds fancy, but the text doesn't mention it. What the disciples threw over the colt was their own cloaks. Then they put Jesus on it (Luke 19:35). I love that. They didn't go shopping, they gave what they were wearing.

explanations.answer: All the miracles they had seen
explanations.explanation: That's it. The whole multitude of disciples praises God joyfully “for all the miracles they had seen.” They weren't praising Him for something they'd heard about secondhand. They'd seen it with their own eyes, and they couldn't keep it in.

That's a reasonable guess for a crowd this loud, friend. But Luke 19:37 says they praise God joyfully “for all the miracles they had seen.” The text gives no battle here. The reason for the noise was the miracles.
A good harvest would be worth some noise, friend. But that's not what the text says. Luke 19:37 says the disciples praised God “for all the miracles they had seen.” That's what had them shouting.
The King! They shout, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” That's a big title to call out loud on a public road. And the one on the colt is the one they're calling it to.
Prophet is a good word, friend, but it's not the one in the crowd's mouth. They shout, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” That word is King. It's right there in Luke 19:38.

Shepherd is a lovely title, friend, and the Bible uses it elsewhere. But here, the crowd shouts, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Luke 19:38). King is the word they use. They said it loud, too.

Rebuke! Some of the Pharisees in the crowd say, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” They call Him Teacher and then ask Him to correct the crowd. That's the request. I think they were hoping for a quiet ride.
Bless would've been a warm request, friend, but that's not what they ask. The Pharisees say, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” (Luke 19:39). Rebuke is the word. Not exactly a thank-you note.

Feed would've been a friendlier ask, friend. But the Pharisees say, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!” That's in Luke 19:39. They weren't asking for anything on a plate, they were asking for a lower volume.

The very stones! Jesus says, “I tell you, if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.” Think about that, friend. Even the rocks on the road have a voice in that sentence. That's a big answer to a small request.
Birds would make a loud choir, friend, but they're not in this verse. Jesus says, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.” Stones. Rocks. The things that never say a word.
Trees are a good guess, friend, since they stand around all day with nothing to say. But Jesus says, “…the very stones will cry out.” That's Luke 19:40. Rocks, not branches.
Wept. Luke 19:41 says that as Jesus approached and saw the city, “He wept over it.” I think this one hurts a little, friend. The crowd was shouting praise, and in the same moment, Jesus weeps.

Singing fits the crowd, friend, but not what the text says about Jesus here. Luke 19:41 says He saw the city and “wept over it.” I think this is a heavy moment. It's a different sound from the road behind Him.
Rejoicing fits all that praise, friend. But the text says that when Jesus saw the city, “He wept over it.” That's Luke 19:41. I think this is one of the quiet, heavy parts of the story.

True. Jesus says, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.” He's talking to the city, and it's a heavy thing to say. I think He says it with tears still on His face, since He just wept over it.

The text says the opposite, friend. Jesus says, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.” That's Luke 19:42. What would bring peace is hidden from the city's eyes.

explanations.answer: It did not recognize God's visit
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jesus gives. He says it will come “because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.” Not a mystery, friend, He tells them plainly. The reason sits right at the end of His words.

explanations.answer: It did not keep the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention the Sabbath here. He says it will come “because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.” That's the reason in Luke 19:44. I'll stick with what He says.

explanations.answer: It made peace with its enemies
explanations.explanation: Close to the topic, friend, but not what He says. Jesus says the enemies will barricade the city and surround it. The reason He gives is “because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.” Peace with enemies never comes up.
